title: US survey foot vs international foot: does it change my grade?
topic: Survey units: survey foot and international foot
text: No. The US survey foot is about 2 parts per million longer than the international foot (0.3048 m exactly), about 0.01 ft per mile, so a cut, a fill, a rod reading or a pipe grade over a run is not changed. Where it matters is state plane coordinates (northings and eastings in the millions of feet), where the two feet can differ by several feet. NGS, NIST and the other federal agencies deprecated the US survey foot on December 31, 2022: from January 1, 2023 it should not be used, and the next state plane system (SPCS2022) supports only the international foot. It stays in older plans and records, and some agency manuals still set up projects in survey feet, so a plan set or data file may still be in survey feet. If a coordinate file and a plan disagree by a few feet over a long distance, ask the surveyor which foot each one uses.
source: Federal Register, Deprecation of the United States (U.S.) Survey Foot, 85 FR 62698 (Oct. 5, 2020), final determination

title: NAVD 88 vs NGVD 29: how far apart are the elevations, and why it matters on a pipe job
topic: Survey: vertical datum
text: Elevations are measured from a vertical datum. Most current plans use NAVD 88; older plans, old record drawings and some local agencies use NGVD 29 (also written NGVD 1929) or a city datum. NGS found NAVD 88 minus NGVD 29 heights range from about -40 cm to +150 cm across the lower 48 states (about -1.3 ft to +4.9 ft), and +94 cm to +240 cm in Alaska. So an invert from an old as-built and a benchmark on the new datum can be off by feet, while every row on the cutsheet still adds up. Before tying into existing pipe or setting up on a benchmark, check that the plans, the cutsheet and the benchmark name the same datum. If they do not, or the benchmark has no datum on it, stop and ask the surveyor or engineer for the conversion. Never convert it yourself from a rule of thumb.
source: Zilkoski, Richards and Young, Results of the General Adjustment of the North American Vertical Datum of 1988, Surveying and Land Information Systems Vol. 52 No. 3 (1992), abstract (published by NGS)

title: Washington WSDOT stake flagging colors and blue tops, red tops, yellow tops
topic: Survey: stake and flagging colors
text: Washington: the WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual (M 22-97, chapter 15) sets flagging colors for construction stakes on WSDOT jobs: clearing and grubbing white, right of way red, slope stakes blue, centerline yellow, drainage blue, signing and illumination white, references and control multicolor, selective thinning orange, trees remaining blue. Spray paint: white is acceptable for stationing along the paved shoulder; pink for all other survey markings, per the national utility color code. Grade hubs (15-02.9): subgrade hubs are called blue tops, base rock hubs red tops, and top course hubs yellow tops. That is different from many other places, where blue top means finish grade, so on a Washington job a blue top may be subgrade. Private surveyors and cities can use their own colors: read the writing on the lath and get the job staking legend. The copy read was dated January 2005 with a draft footer; whether the current WSDOT edition is the same is not confirmed.
source: WSDOT Highway Surveying Manual M 22-97, Chapter 15 Construction Survey Procedures, 15-02.9 and 15-06

title: North Carolina NCDOT construction stake flagging colors and pipe stake cut to invert
topic: Survey: stake and flagging colors
text: North Carolina: the NCDOT Manual for Construction Layout (revised 9/01/2018) gives flagging colors by stake type: centerline orange, slope stakes orange, intermediate grade stakes orange, fine grade hubs orange, clearing limits blue and white striped, ditch stakes blue, pipe stakes blue, minor structure and endwall stakes blue, fence line white, right of way markers white, sign stakes pink, curb stakes orange on the guard stake. Pipe stakes give the cut or fill from the hub to the invert (8.5); pipe stationing starts at 0+00 at the outlet end (8.2). On slope and ditch stakes the manual writes the offset difference with a sign: plus means the offset stake is higher than the intercept point, minus lower (6.5, 7.4). So on NCDOT work a plus or minus on a slope stake is not the same as fill or cut to grade: read the letters and the legend. Private surveyors may use other colors.
source: NCDOT Manual for Construction Layout, revised 9/01/2018, chapters 3-17 (flagging), 6.5, 7.4, 8.2, 8.5

title: Florida Miami-Dade water and sewer jobs: NGVD 1929, NAVD 88 and City of Miami datum on plans
topic: Survey: vertical datum
text: Florida, Miami-Dade Water and Sewer Department (WASD) Section 01031 Grades, Lines and Levels (rev. 5/2017): elevations may be on NGVD 1929, NAVD 88 or the City of Miami datum. WASD accepts NAVD 88 with a conversion factor on each page; it notes FDOT uses NAVD 88 and that City of Miami datum needs a conversion factor to NAVD 88 (3.01-D.8). Stations are set along the pipe centerline (or a stationed offset line) at most 100 ft apart (3.01-B.4), with control points at the start, the end and at least every 1,400 ft (3.01-B.2). For crews: a Miami-Dade plan, an old as-built and a benchmark can be on different datums. Check the datum note and conversion factor on each sheet before tying into existing pipe, and ask the surveyor if they differ.
source: Miami-Dade WASD Design and Construction Standard Specifications, Section 01031 Grades, Lines and Levels, rev. 05/2017, 3.01-B.2, 3.01-B.4, 3.01-D.8

title: Gas or hazardous liquid escaping after you hit a pipeline: the excavator calls 911
topic: Utility strike response
text: Federal pipeline safety rules say that if damage to a pipeline from excavation activity causes the release of any PHMSA regulated natural and other gas or hazardous liquid, "the excavator must promptly report the release to appropriate emergency response authorities by calling the 911 emergency telephone number" (49 CFR 196.109). Get people out and upwind first, keep ignition sources away, then call 911 and the pipeline operator. State one-call laws also require telling the operator about any damage, even a nick; check your state's damage notice rule.
source: 49 CFR 196.109 (Protection of Underground Pipelines From Excavation Activity)

title: Maryland injury reporting to MOSH: deaths in 8 hours, hospital stays in 24 hours
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
text: Maryland employers report a work-related death to MOSH (Maryland Occupational Safety and Health) within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospital stay, an amputation or the loss of an eye within 24 hours. COMAR 09.12.21 adopts the federal recordkeeping and reporting rule, 29 CFR Part 1904, by reference, with MOSH in place of OSHA. MOSH Central Office toll-free number: 1-800-759-6297. Maryland's text words the amputation item as an amputation involving bone or cartilage loss; when in doubt, call. The 8 and 24 hour times are the federal 1904.39 times that COMAR 09.12.21 adopts. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
source: COMAR 09.12.21, Employee Injury and Illness Records and Reports (adopts 29 CFR 1904; amends 1904.39(a)(2))
edition: COMAR 09.12.21 as posted by MOSH, read 2026-11-20

title: Minnesota injury reporting to MNOSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
text: Minnesota employers report every work-related death to MNOSHA within 8 hours, and every work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation and loss of an eye within 24 hours. Call MNOSHA Compliance at 651-284-5050 or 877-470-6742 from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday to Friday; outside those hours, on weekends and holidays, call federal OSHA at 800-321-6742. Minnesota adopted federal OSHA's revised reporting rule effective October 1, 2015. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
source: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry, MNOSHA Compliance: Report an accident, fatality or serious injury

title: Nevada injury reporting to Nevada OSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
text: Nevada employers report to Nevada OSHA (NVOSHA) every workplace accident with an employee death within 8 hours of learning of it, and every in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, amputation, or loss of an eye within 24 hours. Phone: Southern Nevada (702) 486-9020, Northern Nevada (775) 688-3700. These are the same times as the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39). Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
source: Nevada Division of Industrial Relations, Nevada OSHA: Report an Accident or Fatality

title: South Carolina injury reporting to SC OSHA: 8 hours for a death, 24 hours for hospital, amputation, eye
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
text: South Carolina employers report a work-related fatality to SC OSHA within 8 hours, and an in-patient hospitalization, an amputation or an eye loss within 24 hours. Call the SC OSHA office at (803) 896-7672, or report online through the SC OSHA eService portal. These are the same times as the federal rule (29 CFR 1904.39). Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
source: SC Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation, SC OSHA: Report a Severe Injury

title: Iowa injury reporting to Iowa OSHA: federal times, phone 877-242-6742
topic: State safety plan: injury reporting
text: Iowa employers report a work-related death within 8 hours and an in-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours: 875 IAC chapter 4 adopts the federal rule, 29 CFR 1904.0 to 1904.46, by reference. Rule 875-4.3(2) adds ways to report on top of the federal ones: call Iowa OSHA at 877-242-6742, fax or email the completed incident report form, or go to 6200 Park Avenue, Suite 100, Des Moines. Call 911 first for the injured worker; the report is the company's job.
source: Iowa Administrative Code 875 chapter 4 (adopts 29 CFR 1904; rule 4.3(2) reporting methods)

title: California Cal/OSHA trench permit: 5 feet or deeper, annual or project permit, who is exempt
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: California requires a Cal/OSHA permit before building a trench or excavation 5 feet or deeper into which any person is required to descend (8 CCR 341(d)(5)(A)); descend means entering any part of it once it reaches 5 feet. The Project Administrator gets a Project Permit for the project (341(c)(1)); other employers doing the permit work hold an Annual Permit, good for any jobsite that year (341(c)(2)). An Annual Permit holder must notify the Division each time it starts permit-required work at a new site (341(c)(2)(B)). Exempt (341(e)): federal, state, county, city and district government agencies; public utilities under the Public Utilities Commission; trenches for emergency repair of underground facilities; excavations nobody has to enter; graves; swimming pools. Cal/OSHA says annual permit holders must hold a valid contractor's license.
source: 8 CCR 341 (c)(1), (c)(2), (c)(2)(B), (d)(5)(A), (e); Cal/OSHA enforcement FAQ on construction activity permits

title: California toolbox or tailgate safety meetings: at least every 10 working days
topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
text: California construction employers must have supervisors hold toolbox or tailgate safety meetings, or equivalent meetings, with their crews at least every 10 working days to emphasize safety (8 CCR 1509(e)). The same section requires an Injury and Illness Prevention Program under 8 CCR 3203 (1509(a)) and a written Code of Safe Practices for the employer's operations (1509(b)), posted at a conspicuous place at each job site office or given to each supervisor, who keeps it readily available (1509(c)).
source: 8 CCR 1509 (a), (b), (c), (e), Construction Safety Orders

title: Washington crew safety meetings: start of each job and at least weekly, minutes kept 1 year
topic: State safety plan: written programs and training
text: Washington construction employers must hold crew leader-crew safety meetings at the beginning of each job and at least weekly after that (WAC 296-155-110(5)(a)), tailored to the operation. Each meeting covers walk-around inspections, citations and accident investigations since the last meeting (6), and the employer documents attendance (6)(d) and the subjects discussed (6)(e). Minutes of each meeting are prepared and a copy is kept where most of the site's employees report each day (7), and the minutes are kept at least one year (8). Every 2 weeks is not enough in Washington.
source: WAC 296-155-110 (5)(a), (6), (7), (8), Accident prevention program
edition: WAC 296-155-110 as posted by the Legislature, read 2026-11-20

title: Washington first aid card: every crew leader and supervisor needs one
topic: State safety plan: first aid training and emergency numbers
text: Washington requires a person or persons holding a valid first-aid certificate at worksites with a crew (WAC 296-155-120(1)), and crew leaders, supervisors and persons in direct charge of one or more employees must have a valid first-aid certificate (296-155-120(2)). A crew is two or more employees at any worksite (3). A note allows a crew leader to work up to 30 days in an emergency without the certificate if another trained employee or crew leader is in the immediate work area. For a pipe crew this means the foreman carries a current first-aid card.
source: WAC 296-155-120 (1), (2), (3), First-aid requirements

title: California first aid on construction jobs: trained people, a kit, and emergency numbers posted
topic: State safety plan: first aid training and emergency numbers
text: California construction employers must make sure a suitable number of appropriately trained persons are available to give first aid (8 CCR 1512(b)); employers on a shared site may pool them. At least one first-aid kit in a weatherproof container is provided, inspected regularly and restocked (1512(c)(1)); no drugs or medicines unless a physician approves in writing (1512(c)(3)). The phone numbers of a physician and an alternate, hospitals, ambulance services and fire protection services in the area are posted near the job telephone, or otherwise made available where there is no job phone (1512(e)). Section 1512 sets no ratio of first aiders per crew.
source: 8 CCR 1512 (b), (c)(1), (c)(3), (e), Emergency Medical Services
edition: Title 8 section 1512 as posted (last amended 2012), read 2026-11-20

title: California confined space changes from January 1, 2026: site survey and rescue standby
topic: State safety plan: confined space
text: California amended its construction confined space rules (8 CCR 1951, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1956, 1960) effective January 1, 2026. Per the Standards Board's Final Statement of Reasons: a competent person surveys the work area for confined spaces that exist when work begins (1952(a)(1)) and inspects often enough to find new ones (1952(a)(2)); evaluation of a space now includes testing to tell a confined space from a permit space (1952(a)(4)); where less than 10 percent LFL cannot be reached the space is inerted and PPE provided (1953); and standby personnel trained, equipped and available to rescue an entrant are required (1960(a)). The Final Statement of Reasons describes no change to the permit items in 1955. Read the amended rule text before relying on wording.
source: OSHSB rulemaking Confined Spaces in Construction, Final Statement of Reasons updated 2025-09-18; effective 2026-01-01

title: Michigan confined space in construction: MIOSHA Part 35 adopts the federal rule
topic: State safety plan: confined space
text: Michigan's Construction Safety Standard Part 35, Confined Space in Construction, adopts 29 CFR 1926.1202 (definitions) through 1926.1212 (employee participation) by reference, except as amended in the rules (R 408.43510, via the scope rule R 408.43501(4)). That includes the federal permit items in 1926.1206, so a federal-style entry permit covers Michigan. Part 35 does not apply to work covered by Part 9 (excavation, trenching and shoring), Part 14 (tunnels, shafts, caissons, cofferdams), Part 504 (diving) or Part 665 (underground construction and compressed air); where another standard also covers a confined space hazard, both apply (R 408.43501(2), (3)). Part 35 has three rules: scope, provision of documents, and adopted standards.
source: Mich. Admin. Code R 408.43501, R 408.43505, R 408.43510 (MIOSHA Part 35)
edition: Part 35 as posted by Cornell LII, read 2026-11-20

title: Indiana trench protection: IOSHA adopts the federal excavation rule, 5 feet
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: Indiana adopts the federal excavation rule, 29 CFR 1926.650 through 1926.652 with Appendices A to F, by reference (620 IAC 1-1-30, items 7 and 18; effective in Indiana March 5, 1990). So a trench 5 feet or deeper needs a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a shield) unless it is entirely in stable rock, and a competent person inspects daily (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1), 1926.651(k)). The adopting rule shows no Indiana depth, permit or other excavation requirement of its own. OSHA's Indiana state plan page lists a unique excavation standard; it was not identified, so ask IOSHA if a job depends on it (not confirmed).
source: 620 IAC 1-1-30 (adoption by reference from 54 FR, 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P)

title: Maryland trench rule: federal 5 feet, plus protective system records kept at the jobsite
topic: State safety plan: trench and excavation
text: Maryland (MOSH) uses the federal excavation rule: a protective system from 5 feet unless the trench is entirely in stable rock (29 CFR 1926.652). Maryland amends 1926.652 on records: the tabulated data used for a protective system, a slope design, the manufacturer's data and any approval to deviate from it, and an engineer's design are kept at the jobsite while the system is being built and after that until it is no longer used; then they may be kept off site but available to the Commissioner of Labor and Industry on request (Maryland amendments to 1926.652(b)(4)(iii), (c)(2)(iii), (c)(4)(iii)). MOSH lists no Maryland supplement to the confined space in construction rule.
source: MOSH, Maryland amendments to 29 CFR 1926.652; MOSH-specific standards list

title: Colorado: new underground lines must be electronically locatable (tracer wire on PVC)
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: Colorado law requires all new underground facilities installed on or after August 8, 2018 to be electronically locatable, including laterals up to the building they serve (C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(10)). The Colorado Underground Damage Prevention Safety Commission says the install method does not change this (pipe bursting counts), planned replacement or rehab is treated as new work, and routine repairs are not included. For PVC and other pipe a locator cannot find, a tracer wire or another locating method is part of the design and install; the Commission does not pick the method. If a tracer wire is cut, repair it or otherwise keep the line locatable. Your project spec sets the wire type, splices and test stations.
source: C.R.S. 9-1.5-103(10), as quoted in Colorado UDPSC Best Practice "Electronically Locatable" (approved 2019-11-14)

title: Indiana: new or replacement underground lines must be detectable (locating wire on nonmetallic pipe)
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: Indiana law (IC 8-1-26-18.5) covers any new or replacement underground facility installed after June 30, 2020, in public right-of-way or on private property. The operator (whoever installs it or has it installed) must make sure it can be detected from above ground. If the material cannot be found with standard locating equipment, as with PVC or HDPE, the facility must be encased in conductive material or equipped with an electrically conducting wire or other means of locating it underground. In practice that means tracer wire on plastic water and sewer pipe unless the plans call for another method. The section does not list exceptions such as sewer laterals in the text read; check with the owner or engineer.
source: Indiana Code 8-1-26-18.5 (read at FindLaw; verify the current text at iga.in.gov)

title: West Virginia: underground lines installed since July 1, 2018 must be locatable
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: West Virginia law (W. Va. Code 24C-1-11) says underground facilities owned by an operator and installed on or after July 1, 2018 must be installed so they are locatable using a generally accepted locating method. The law does not name a method; for PVC, HDPE and other nonmetallic pipe that usually means tracer wire or another method the owner accepts. The project spec and the utility owner set the wire, splices and test points.
source: W. Va. Code 24C-1-11 (West Virginia Legislature)

title: Nebraska: plastic and nonmetallic lines installed since 2021 must be locatable (mapping or tracer wire)
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: Nebraska law (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-2320.02) says plastic or nonmetallic underground facilities installed on or after January 1, 2021 must be installed so the operator can locate them under the One-Call Notification System Act, either by mapping or by tracer wire. The owner picks which; ask before you lay plastic pipe whether tracer wire is required. This was read from a 2020 compilation, so the current wording is not confirmed; check it on the Nebraska Legislature site.
source: Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-2320.02 (2020 compilation read at Justia; current text at nebraskalegislature.gov not read)

title: Minnesota: nonconductive lines in public right-of-way need a locating wire (Rule 7560.0150)
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: Minnesota Rule 7560.0150, subpart 2: for each nonconductive underground facility installed in a public right-of-way after December 31, 2005, the operator must install a locating wire (tracer wire) or an equally effective means of marking where it is. Minor repairs, meaning repairs to or partial replacement of existing service laterals for routine upkeep, are not covered. Subpart 1 also has operators keep records (map, drawing or GIS) of facilities they install in public right-of-way. This is the 2014 version of the rule as read; the current version is not confirmed, so check it at revisor.mn.gov.
source: Minnesota Rules 7560.0150, subparts 1 and 2 (version of 2014-01-18 at revisor.mn.gov)

title: Gas lines: plastic pipe must have a tracer wire or other way to locate it (49 CFR 192.321(e))
topic: Locatable pipe: tracer wire and locating rules
text: Federal gas pipeline rule 49 CFR 192.321(e): "Plastic pipe that is not encased must have an electrically conducting wire or other means of locating the pipe while it is underground." Tracer wire may not be wrapped around the pipe, contact with the pipe should be kept small, and the wire must resist corrosion (coated copper or another means). This rule is for gas transmission lines and mains. Water and sewer tracer wire comes from state law in some states and from the project spec everywhere else.
source: 49 CFR 192.321(e), Installation of plastic pipe (eCFR / LII)

title: Minnesota 811: when can I dig after I file a ticket (48 hours, the filing day not counted)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Minnesota: wait at least 48 hours before digging, and the 48 hours do not count the day you file the ticket, Saturdays, Sundays or holidays (Minn. Stat. 216D.04). Gopher State One Call says the 48 hours begin at 12:01 a.m. on the business day after the request. So a ticket filed on a Tuesday can be dug on Friday, and one filed on a Friday can be dug the next Wednesday, when there is no holiday in between. File no more than 14 calendar days ahead. The ticket is good for 14 calendar days from the start date and time printed on it. An Update gets a new ticket number and its own 48-hour wait, so send it early enough to keep digging without a gap. Go by the start date and time on your ticket.
source: Gopher State One Call web page "when can I dig" (read Nov 20, 2026); Minn. Stat. 216D.04

title: Iowa 811: when can I dig after I call (the 48 hours start 6 AM the next business day)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Iowa: the law defines the forty-eight-hour wait as beginning at 6:00 a.m. on the next business day after Iowa One Call receives the notice, and it skips Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays (Iowa Code 480.1(6), 480.4). So a notice given on a Monday can be dug from 6:00 a.m. Thursday, and one given on a Friday from 6:00 a.m. the next Wednesday, when there is no holiday in between. The notice is valid for 25 calendar days beginning on the day the 48-hour period ends. There is no renewal: ask for a new ticket before the old one runs out, and it has the same wait.
source: Iowa Code 480.1(6) and 480.4 (Iowa Code 2026, chapter 480)

title: Indiana 811: when can I dig after I call (2 full working days, then 7 AM)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Indiana: call at least two full working days and not more than ten calendar days before digging (Ind. Code 8-1-26-16). The day you call is not a full working day. Work may start at 7 a.m. on the next working day after the two full working days, so a Monday call can be dug from 7 a.m. Thursday when there is no holiday in between. You may start sooner only if every operator has posted a positive response. A notice expires at 11:59 p.m. twenty days after it is received.
source: Ind. Code 8-1-26-16

title: South Dakota 811: when can I dig after I call (the 48 hours start 12:01 AM the next day)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: South Dakota: give notice at least 48 hours before digging. Under SDCL 49-7A-5 as amended in 2026 (Senate Bill 9), the 48 hours start at 12:01 a.m. on the day after the notice and skip Saturdays, Sundays and state legal holidays. So a notice given on a Monday can be dug Thursday, when there is no holiday in between. Marks are good while clearly visible, but not more than 21 calendar days from the start date on the ticket.
source: SDCL 49-7A-5 as amended by 2026 Senate Bill 9; ARSD 20:25:03:05.01

title: Oklahoma 811: when can I dig after I call (48 hours, the call day not counted)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Oklahoma: give notice at least 48 hours before digging, not counting the day of the notice, Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. So a notice given on a Monday can be dug Thursday when there is no holiday in between. Demolition needs 7 business days.
source: OKIE811 Excavator Guide, February 2026 (law text as of Nov 1, 2025), 63 O.S. 142.4 and 142.6

title: South Carolina 811: when can I dig after I call (3 full working days) and SC811 holidays
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: South Carolina: operators have three full working days to mark, not counting the day you call, so a Monday call can be dug Friday when there is no holiday in between. SC811's 2026 holiday list adds days that do not count toward the three full working days even though the center is open: Confederate Memorial Day (May 11, 2026), Christmas Eve (December 24) and the day after Christmas (observed December 28, 2026); the notice is counted from the next business day. Its other 2026 holidays are New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Memorial Day, Independence Day (July 3), Labor Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving and the day after, and Christmas. Columbus Day and Juneteenth are not on the list.
source: SC811 2026 Holidays page (read Nov 20, 2026); SC811 Excavator Manual 2026

title: Nevada 811: which holidays don't count as working days for a ticket (USA North 811)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Nevada: working days leave out Saturdays, Sundays and federal or state holidays (NRS 455.105). USA North 811's holiday list for Nevada in 2026: New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day (observed July 3), Labor Day, Nevada Day (the last Friday of October, October 30, 2026), Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, Family Day (the Friday after Thanksgiving) and Christmas. Columbus Day is not on the Nevada list. A holiday on a Saturday is observed the Friday before; one on a Sunday, the Monday after. Go by the start date on your ticket.
source: USA North 811 "List of Holidays" page (read Nov 20, 2026); NRS 455.105

title: Utah 811: which holidays don't count for ticket times (Blue Stakes)
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Utah: Blue Stakes of Utah 811 treats these 2026 days as closed for all ticket date and time calculations: New Year's Day, Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Presidents' Day, Memorial Day, Juneteenth, Independence Day (observed July 3), Pioneer Day (July 24), Labor Day, Columbus Day, Veterans Day, Thanksgiving, the day after Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve and Christmas. The center is open on Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Juneteenth, Columbus Day and Veterans Day but still counts them as closed. Its holiday definition covers the legal holidays in Utah Code 63G-1-301, the Friday after Thanksgiving, December 24 and any other day the association observes.
source: Blue Stakes of Utah 811, Holiday Closures 2026 (PDF, read Nov 20, 2026)

title: Oregon 811: ticket life is 30 days (changed from 45 in 2026), no renewals
topic: 811 tickets: types, ticket life, renewals and updates
text: Oregon: a locate ticket is good for 30 calendar days. The Oregon Utility Notification Center's 2026 Addendum to the Oregon Standards Manual lists the change to OAR 952-001-0010(23), "from 45 days to 30 days," effective January 8, 2026, and the center's homeowner page says marks "should no longer be used after 30 days." Older copies of the rule still say 45. There is no renewal: to keep digging after 30 days, re-notify the center with a new locate request and the normal wait of 2 full business days (a request after 5 p.m. counts as the next business day). Do not start more than 10 business days after the notice without re-notifying. Keep the marks up for the life of the job or of the ticket, whichever is shorter. Marks gone: stop and ask for a remark. There is no legal "priority" locate.
source: 2026 Addendum to the Oregon Standards Manual (OAR 952-001-0010(23), effective Jan 8, 2026); Oregon 811 homeowners page (read Nov 20, 2026)

title: New national vertical datum (NAPGD2022) replacing NAVD 88: what changes for elevations
topic: Survey: vertical datum
text: NGS is replacing NAVD 88 with the North American-Pacific Geopotential Datum of 2022 (NAPGD2022), part of the modernized National Spatial Reference System. A NOAA summary (2019) says the new vertical datum will change heights by about 50 cm on average, with about a 1 m tilt toward the Pacific Northwest. NGS says it is rolling the new system out for public testing over 2024 to 2026, the Federal Geodetic Control Subcommittee is expected to vote on approval (likely mid 2026), and the current system stays official during the rollout; NGS stops taking new submissions to the current system after January 13, 2027. Whether approval has happened is not confirmed here. For crews: once agencies switch, new plans and old as-builts may be on different datums by a foot or more. Check the datum note on every plan sheet and benchmark.
source: NGS New Datums FAQ (geodesy.noaa.gov/datums/newdatums/FAQNewDatums.shtml); NOAA HSRP one-pager, New Datums (2019)

title: Tennessee TDOT survey units and datum: US survey foot state plane, NAVD 88, Geoid 18
topic: Survey units: survey foot and international foot
text: Tennessee: the TDOT Survey Standards Manual (Fourth Edition, October 2023) sets TDOT project control on NAD 83 (2011) Tennessee State Plane in US survey feet (2.1.3.1), vertical control on NAVD 88 for all TDOT projects, and Geoid 18 as the default geoid model unless directed otherwise (2.1.3.1). So TDOT plans after the federal retirement of the survey foot (December 31, 2022) still use survey feet for coordinates. That does not change cuts, fills or pipe grades; it matters only when mixing TDOT coordinates with data in international feet. Ask the TDOT Regional Survey Coordinator or the project surveyor.
source: TDOT Survey Standards Manual, Fourth Edition, October 2023, 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.1.3.1

title: Arizona ADOT slope stakes: how cut and fill are written
topic: Survey: stake writing
text: Arizona: the ADOT Construction Manual, Section 1109 Construction Surveying (January 2005), says the standard slope stake is 1 in x 2 in x 14 in. On a cut, the inside of the slope stake carries the letter C, the cut at that point, the horizontal distance from centerline and the slope ratio (1109-3). On a fill, the front face carries the letter F, the fill from the guinea to grade, the distance from centerline to the guinea and the fill slope ratio (1109-4). The station is on the back. Offsets are measured at right angles from centerline to 0.01 ft; rod readings to 0.1 ft. ADOT coding and placement of slope stakes is in Exhibit 1109-1-1 (not read here).
source: ADOT Construction Manual, Chapter 11, Section 1109 Construction Surveying, January 2005, 1109-3, 1109-4
